sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
October 2026 delivered a sharply bifurcated global equity tape, with technology-sensitive indices bearing the heaviest losses while value-oriented and energy-exposed benchmarks held their ground or advanced. The S&P 500 retreated **0.87%** to close at **7,580**, having reached an all-time high of **7,818.93** on October 6 before a broadening tech rout erased early gains. The Dow Jones Industrial Average bucked the trend, gaining **1.76%** to close at **51,770** as defensives and energy names outperformed.

The Nasdaq Composite fell **5.28%** — its worst monthly decline since March 2025 — as investors repriced the near-term earnings potential of artificial intelligence investments. In Asia, the Nikkei 225 shed **5.2%**, the Hang Seng declined **5.36%**, and the Shanghai Composite fell approximately **6.3%** amid ongoing uncertainty around Chinese domestic demand. European bourses proved considerably more resilient, with the FTSE 100 and DAX each gaining **1.2%**, supported by their structural overweight in energy producers and financial stocks.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes: AI Mega-Capex Under the Microscope -- The singular force depressing global risk appetite in October was mounting investor scepticism toward the AI capital expenditure cycle. Mega-cap technology earnings — most notably Meta, Alphabet, and Amazon — delivered results that highlighted ballooning infrastructure costs against muted near-term AI revenue, triggering a **5.28%** monthly collapse in the Nasdaq Composite, its worst showing since March 2025. Meta's widely-cited beat obscured billions in undisclosed legal penalties, while Nvidia's forward revenue outlook — with its earnings slated for November 17 — became the central proxy for investor conviction in the AI demand thesis. The equal-weight S&P 500 materially outperformed the cap-weighted index, confirming that the derating was concentrated at the mega-cap AI layer rather than the broader market.

Iran and the Strait of Hormuz Oil Shock -- Geopolitical risk re-entered commodity markets with force in October as reports of renewed US and Israeli strikes on Iranian targets circulated alongside a surge in shipping attacks near the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude surged approximately **14%** over the month to close near **$116/bbl** (approx., verify before merging), marking its steepest monthly advance in over a year, while WTI settled at **$104.12** on October 30. Energy equities emerged as among the month's top-performing sectors globally, with FTSE 100 oil majors and US energy producers leading the rotation. The oil shock complicated the Federal Reserve's policy calculus by injecting a fresh supply-side inflationary impulse at precisely the moment that slowing AI-driven corporate investment was cooling demand-side growth expectations.

Treasury Yield Surge and the Flight-to-Quality Reversal -- Fixed income markets experienced exceptional two-way volatility in October, with the 10-year US Treasury yield surging to a cycle high of **5.36%** on October 7 — its highest level since April 2002 — before retreating sharply to close the month near **4.94%**. The late-month rally was dramatic: a single-session decline of **19.3 basis points** on October 22 was the largest one-day drop in the 10-year since March 2023, coinciding with peak equity market stress. The 2-year yield ended October near **4.69%**, leaving the 10-2 spread positive at roughly **+25 basis points** — confirming the yield curve's sustained return from inversion for the first time since mid-2024. The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady at its October meeting, citing stagflationary crosscurrents arising from elevated energy prices and softening growth.

Factor Rotation: Value and Defensives Displace Growth -- October crystallised a regime shift in equity factor leadership that had been building since summer, as the spread between growth and value reached its widest level in several years. The Dow's **+1.76%** gain versus the Nasdaq's **-5.28%** loss represented a monthly gap of over **700 basis points** between the two most-watched US benchmarks, with institutional flows moving aggressively into value, defensives, and energy. European bourses, with their structural overweight in banks, energy majors, and industrials, outperformed their US growth-heavy counterparts by a wide margin, reinforcing the cross-asset rotation narrative. The shift in factor leadership was accompanied by a surge in demand for Nasdaq 100 put protection and a rise in implied volatility across technology names, underscoring the breadth of institutional repositioning underway heading into year-end.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equity markets entered October at record levels before an AI-driven derating compressed valuation multiples across the technology sector. The S&P 500 set its cycle high at **7,818.93** on October 6 before declining **0.87%** for the month to close at **7,580**, while the Nasdaq's **5.28%** monthly loss was its steepest since March 2025. The Dow Jones Industrial Average proved the exception, rising **1.76%** to close at **51,770** as energy producers and defensive industrials attracted renewed institutional demand.

Earnings season supplied the proximate catalyst for the drawdown. Meta's headline beat masked billions in legal penalties; Alphabet and Amazon flagged persistent AI infrastructure costs with muted near-term revenue offsets; and Intel's results highlighted ongoing competitive pressure in the semiconductor landscape. With Nvidia's earnings scheduled for November 17, investor anxiety over whether the AI capital expenditure cycle would translate into commensurate revenue returns dominated sector sentiment throughout the month.

The equal-weight S&P 500 meaningfully outperformed its cap-weighted counterpart, confirming that the drawdown was concentrated among mega-cap technology names rather than the broader market. Defensive sectors — utilities, consumer staples, and healthcare — attracted sustained inflows as institutional investors rotated toward less rate-sensitive and less AI-exposed positions, foreshadowing a potential leadership shift heading into year-end.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets demonstrated notable resilience in October, with the FTSE 100 and DAX both advancing **1.2%** while the CAC 40 finished essentially flat at **+0.06%**. The outperformance relative to US growth indices reflected structural composition differences: European benchmarks carry a heavier weighting in energy producers, industrials, and financials — all of which benefited from elevated oil prices and a steepening yield curve. The FTSE 100 closed October near **10,730** (approx., verify before merging), supported by oil majors BP and Shell as Brent crude surged on Middle East supply risk.

The DAX benefited from resilient industrial order data and a stabilisation in German manufacturing confidence, while the CAC 40 was partially restrained by concerns over French fiscal sustainability and sovereign spread widening relative to German Bunds. The ECB, acknowledging that core inflation remained sticky against the backdrop of elevated energy prices, telegraphed a cautious stance that lent additional support to European financial stocks. Regional banks and insurance companies were among the strongest-performing sub-sectors, responding favourably to the steeper yield curve environment.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian equity markets bore the brunt of October's global risk-off rotation, with technology-heavy benchmarks suffering their most significant monthly declines of the year. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell **5.2%**, partly reversing its exceptional year-to-date gains, as the yen's continued depreciation against the dollar complicated the Bank of Japan's policy signalling and triggered systematic profit-taking in export-oriented names. Currency dynamics created an unusual feedback loop: yen weakness that historically supported Japanese exporters was now viewed as a liability, forcing the BoJ into an uncomfortable balancing act between supporting growth and defending currency credibility.

The Hang Seng declined **5.36%** to close near **23,294**, bringing its year-to-date loss to approximately **-9.11%**, as investor confidence in Chinese technology and property sector recovery faded amid disappointing consumption data and continued regulatory uncertainty. The Shanghai Composite shed approximately **6.3%** for the month as domestic stimulus measures failed to offset weakness in property-linked financials and softening export volumes. Across the region, the APAC selloff underscored the dual vulnerability of Asian markets to US dollar strength and global technology sector sentiment deterioration.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar was broadly stable in October despite significant equity market volatility, with the DXY index ending the month near **101.88** — roughly unchanged to marginally lower for the period (approx., verify before merging). The greenback's relative steadiness reflected competing forces: risk-off demand provided support, while the Fed's decision to hold rates steady and the equity outflows into Treasuries partially dampened the yield-spread argument for further dollar appreciation. EUR/USD ended the month near **1.1206**, finding support above **1.1100** despite French fiscal concerns weighing on the pair's upside.

GBP/USD held firmer, closing near **1.3397**, underpinned by the Bank of England's hawkish tone and tighter-than-expected UK labour market data. The most notable move in G10 FX was USD/JPY, which continued its ascent to close near **157.56** as the Bank of Japan resisted pressure to accelerate its policy normalisation timeline despite yen depreciation concerns. The pair's sustained elevation drew increasingly pointed commentary from Japanese finance officials and raised market speculation about potential currency intervention, though no concrete action materialised during October.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Energy markets dominated commodity headlines in October, with oil staging its largest monthly rally in over a year on severe Middle East supply disruption fears. Brent crude surged approximately **14%** to close near **$116/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) as shipping attacks near the Strait of Hormuz intensified and reports of renewed US/Israeli strikes on Iranian targets circulated; WTI crude settled at **$104.12** on October 30, confirming the synchronised nature of the move across the complex. The oil price surge set up fresh inflationary impulses for November consumer price data and weighed on the global growth outlook, particularly for oil-importing economies in Asia.

Gold reversed sharply, falling approximately **6–7%** to close around **$3,900/oz** (approx., verify before merging) after breaking below the psychologically important **$4,000** level in late October. The pullback reflected the dual headwinds of an on-hold Federal Reserve and the surge in real Treasury yields during the month's first half, which collectively eroded gold's non-yielding asset appeal. Copper demonstrated underlying resilience, with LME cash settling at **$14,449/tonne** on October 30 and retaining a year-to-date gain of **15.6%** — a signal that the commodity markets' AI-driven infrastructure buildout narrative remained structurally intact despite the equity-level repricing of AI expectations.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
October was an extraordinary month for US Treasuries, characterised first by a dramatic yield surge to multi-year highs and then by an equally sharp reversal as equity market stress drove a flight to quality. The 10-year Treasury yield opened October near **4.80%** before spiking to a cycle high of **5.36%** on October 7 — its highest level since April 2002 — before retreating to close the month near **4.94%**. The 2-year yield followed a similar arc, ending October near **4.69%**, implying a 10-2 spread of roughly **+25 basis points** and confirming the yield curve's first sustained return to positive territory since mid-2024.

The late-month bond market rally was punctuated by the 10-year's single-session fall of **19.3 basis points** on October 22 — the largest one-day drop since March 2023 — coinciding directly with peak equity market stress as the AI-tech rout accelerated. The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady at its October meeting, acknowledging stagflationary crosscurrents arising from elevated energy prices and slowing corporate investment growth. Market pricing for the December FOMC shifted toward a prolonged hold, with futures implying no rate cut before mid-2027 — a repricing that added duration to the fixed income rally as month-end approached.
